To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“Pathological aging, as opposed to normal aging, is characterized by a lack of compensatory mechanisms that are instead present in normal aging.
the brain of the aged is less resilient to the effects of pathology than the brain of the young.

(1) pathological aging does not lead to compensation; (2) in pathological aging, the brain is less able to compensate for the effects of lesions; (3) pathological aging is associated with less efficient brain networks, and with the lack of compensation.

the investigation of brain mechanisms involved in the processing of visuo-spatial information.
the study of the neural correlates of the cognitive and emotional changes associated with aging.
the study of brain mechanisms of cognitive functions in healthy aging, and in pathological aging.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the present study shows that, in the absence of a clear and unequivocal diagnosis, the use of neuroimaging techniques is not sufficient to identify the presence of a neurodegenerative disease, but that a careful and thorough neuropsychological examination, which includes the analysis of the cognitive and behavioral profile of the patient, may be useful in the diagnostic process.

the brain of the aged individual is characterized by a loss of neurons, a loss of synaptic connections, and a loss of functional connectivity, which is reflected by a loss of efficiency in the performance of cognitive tasks.

, although the present study is not conclusive, it does suggest that, in the absence of any compensatory mechanisms, the brain of the aged subject may not be able to maintain the same level of performance as that of a young person in tasks involving complex cognitive processes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

1) the brain of healthy elderly subjects is characterized by the presence of compensatory mechanisms that allow them to perform tasks that are difficult for young people; 2) the brain of pathological elderly subjects is characterized instead by the absence of compensatory mechanisms, which makes it difficult for them to perform tasks of any kind, even those that young subjects can perform easily; 3) the absence of compensating mechanisms is due to a lack of brain plasticity.
the aging brain is a very complex and dynamic organ, and it is not possible to define the brain as a whole in terms of its functional and morphological characteristics.
the brain is a highly plastic organ that is capable of adapting to the environment, and that this plasticity is not limited to the early stages of life, as previously assumed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the aging brain can be considered pathological, in the sense that the neural substrate of the cognitive processes does not change as a function of the cognitive demand.
, in the absence of pathological lesions, the aging brain is characterized by an absence of compensatory mechanisms.
pathological aging, as opposed to normal aging, is characterized by an impairment of cognitive control mechanisms.
